extracted.intended_audience: pre-service middle school teachers and mathematics teacher-educators / university mathematics faculty
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and running capstone precalculus and calculus courses that vertically connect college-level content to middle grades mathematics for pre-service middle school teachers, including active-learning activities, assessment practices, and final projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link geometric and functional transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Have students explore transformations first geometrically (on grid/paper/manipulatives) and then functionally, e.g., translating a labeled figure and recording coordinates, then translating graphs of functions and expressing the change in function notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use manipulatives (patty paper) and coordinate notation exercises: write coordinates of vertices, perform translations (e.g., left 4, down 1), describe in words and symbols, and generalize to coordinate notation (T(x,y) -> (x-4,y-1)). Then translate the idea to functions (e.g., f(x)=x^2 shifted) and have students check via graphing calculator. Emphasize making the connection explicit because horizontal translations can be confusing when switching between coordinate and function notation; require deep thinking about the 'turned around' functional point of view so pre-service teachers can anticipate student misconceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative approach to exponentials and logarithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a conceptual basis for exponentials and logarithms by focusing on their inverse relationship and using qualitative/numerical methods rather than immediately relying on calculator log-button.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students solve exponential equations numerically (e.g., 10^x = 60) using graphing, guess-and-check, or bisection methods, and require them to show how they obtained solutions graphically or numerically. Pre- and post-testing showed such approaches improve understanding that a logarithm is an exponent and how log properties follow from exponent properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of calculus worksheets to discover concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the calculus course around a sequence of guided problem-set worksheets that lead students from limits to applications of integration, designed for discovery of concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use roughly one worksheet per week (18 problem sets for a semester), have the instructor spend 1–2 minutes introducing each set, have students work in small groups during class, and wrap up with whole-class discussion where students share solutions and the instructor guides identification of the 'big ideas' of each set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question-of-the-day practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Daily brief question or topic connecting course content to middle school mathematics, discussed as a group and assigned for journal write-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor selects or allows emergent questions tied to the content of the day. Discuss the question briefly in class, then assign students to write and submit an explanation as a journal entry. Use questions that force students to return to first principles and that produce discussion, arguments, presentations, and 'aha' moments. Examples include conceptual prompts about dividing by zero, the meaning of radical signs, resolving apparent contradictions between coordinate and function notation for shifts, inequality reversal when multiplying by negatives, and meanings of inverse-function notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal grading rubric (7/9/10)
rubrics_metrics.description: A concise scoring rubric for journals responding to questions or video case prompts: 7 points, 9 points, 10 points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 7 points: effort was made but the response is incomplete or incoherent. 9 points: ideas are coherent and communicated well. 10 points: writer goes above and beyond, showing deep reflection and insight. Journals graded by this rubric count toward the written-work portion of the course grade (stated as 25% in the course).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of video case studies with preparatory readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Have students view short (≈15 minute) video excerpts of middle school classrooms accompanied by written commentaries and require journal responses and discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign the accompanying written commentaries (from Connecting Mathematical Ideas) as readings prior to viewing to enhance discussion. After viewing, hold small and large group discussions and require journals responding to selected prompts from the discussion guides. Grade journals using the 7/9/10 rubric. Video cases model close attention to student thinking and tying mathematics to pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select middle school curriculum excerpts to highlight vertical connections
rubrics_metrics.description: For each college-level content topic, present samples/excerpts from middle school curricula that connect to the topic and discuss the connections with students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose curriculum excerpts where connections are obvious (e.g., slope via coordinate table versus derivative approximation) or less obvious (e.g., patterns/sequences to trigonometric periodicity). Present excerpts after studying the college topic and facilitate large-group discussion (not graded) to identify connections; provide copies or links if students can't access local curricula and encourage students to bring local district texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-problem comparison final paper requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Final summative written assignment where each student selects a college-level problem and a related grade-4–8 problem and analyzes the mathematical connections between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both problems must be approved by the instructor (require early submission of proposed problems). The student must solve both problems and provide a thorough explanation including strategies used, context, and identification of applicable mathematics standards (Texas Essential Knowledge and Skills). The analysis should clarify the common ideas (algorithmic, structural, strategic, superficial), and a sample assignment sheet and student checklist should be provided to guide writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require instructor approval and early proposal for major projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should submit proposed problems early in the semester for instructor approval to ensure selected problems are rich enough for analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend early submission and approval so projects are sufficiently substantive and instructors can guide selection toward problems that yield deep connections rather than superficial ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model classroom pedagogy: active, hands-on, guided discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach K–8 mathematics education courses (and the College Algebra for Teachers course) using hands-on guided discovery, activity-based instruction, and small-group work led by mathematics faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure class meetings (e.g., two 110-minute sessions per week) to include brief question-answer/quiz, small-group reading of an activity set, instructor lead-in activity, circulating facilitation (answering with questions), and whole-class sharing of observations. Encourage and discuss effective group-work and sharing strategies explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student Activity Set structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Each student Activity Set should include a Purpose, list of Student Materials, and an Introduction with background, definitions, examples, drawing guides, graphing-calculator instructions, and exploration activities with space for students to write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow each Activity Set with homework, and end chapters with a Review and Vocabulary Guide and a Student Practice Chapter Exam. Make selected answers and practice-exam answers available to support student learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor Resource Manual content
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor notes and resources should accompany student materials and provide pedagogical scaffolding for each Activity Set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include Topic Significance, the Purpose, Instructor Materials, a Lead-In Activity to set the stage, pedagogical notes on cooperative student work, ideas for Follow-Up Class Discussion, homework comments and assignment suggestions, overhead masters, and Instructor Chapter Exams with solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete models to teach integer operations and integer-subtraction rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with black-and-red tile models to represent +1 and −1 to build intuition about integer collections and rules such as 'subtracting a negative is adding'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students construct zero pairs and other tile collections to show why subtracting negatives results in addition (e.g., add five zero-pairs and remove red tiles to see net effect). Use these visual/concrete demonstrations before abstract rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Progression and scope limits for algebra-piece modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequence modeling from whole-number variable strips to rational coefficients and then to real-number/ quadratic modeling using different colored strips and squares; initially constrain modeling to problems that fit the manipulatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with whole-number linear expressions and equations using black 'n-strips' (always positive) and red strips (always negative). Initially focus on one-variable linear equations with integer coefficients and constants; after mastery, extend to rational coefficients and discuss methods for handling fractions. For quadratics, introduce white variable strips (x and −x) and variable squares (x^2) to model ax^2+bx+c, then use factor-rectangle construction to teach factoring, intercepts, turning points, and ranges. Demonstrate failed arrangements as pedagogical tools (showing what doesn't work) to deepen structural reasoning.
